strengths: The paper provides a genuine theoretical contribution: it proves last-iterate convergence to the (unregularized) Nash equilibrium of the two-player zero-sum game, whereas prior iterative methods (iterative IPO, SPPO, Nash-MD, INPO) only achieve average-iterate convergence or converge to a KL-regularized modified game that does not yield the robust-alignment (50% win-rate) guarantee. Theorem 1, Theorem 2 (linear convergence of the regularized solver), and Theorem 3 (convergence under approximate solutions) are non-trivial and carefully proved in the appendices.

The unification of diverse preference-optimization algorithms (PPO, DPO, IPO, SPPO, REBEL, DRO, INPO) as implementations of the prox operator is elegant and practically useful: it lets COVAL be plugged in over existing methods as a black box with minimal change, which lowers the barrier to adoption.

The synthetic 3x3 intransitive-preference experiment cleanly isolates the phenomenon: it shows MD/iterative-IPO/SPPO cycling while COVAL converges to the unique Nash equilibrium in last iterate, providing crisp empirical support for the theory.

The paper is well organized, clearly written, and includes substantial appendix material (proofs, hyperparameter search, additional results), and the code/models are stated to be released, which supports reproducibility.

The LLM-based study goes beyond prior work by running up to 42 iterations (7 full passes over UltraFeedback), and the comparison tables (Table 2, Table 4) demonstrate that COVAL attains >50% win rate against every baseline and the best average, illustrating the stability benefit of repeatedly updating the reference policy.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is limited. COVAL is essentially the conceptual prox-method / iterative-regularization scheme (Nesterov 2004; Nemirovski 2004) applied to the alignment game. The paper is transparent about this, but the core algorithmic idea is a known game-theoretic technique rather than a new mechanism, so the contribution rests largely on applying it and re-framing existing methods.

The evaluation protocol is questionable: the preference oracle used to generate pairwise training data (Llama-3-OffsetBias-8B) is also used as the evaluator. This creates a self-consistent/controlled loop in which the policy is optimized against the very model that scores it, so the reported win rates do not demonstrate generalization to real human preferences or to an independent judge. At minimum, an independent evaluator (e.g., GPT-4 or human judgments) should corroborate the ranking.

The empirical gains are modest and lack statistical grounding. In Table 2 COVAL scores only 50.00-55.90 against INPO-Small/INPO-Large and wins by ~1-3 points over other strong baselines; no seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported, so it is unclear whether differences exceed run-to-run noise.

Experiments are narrow: a single 1.5B model (Qwen2-1.5B), a single dataset (UltraFeedback), and no human evaluation or comparison to large-scale RLHF/PPO pipelines. No ablation isolates how much of the gain comes from the meta-algorithm versus from the underlying INPO sub-solver, and the COVAL-specific hyperparameter schedule (updating the reference policy when the first optimization step converges/overfits, switching eta^-1 from 0.002 to 0.01) appears tuned per-setting, raising reproducibility concerns.

The robust-alignment guarantee is a property of the exact Nash equilibrium; the practical algorithm only computes approximate solutions, and the paper reports a plain point where the objective can still fall short of the guarantee. Table 2 shows COVAL barely exceeding 50% in several pairings (50.00, 51.30, 55.16), which is within plausible noise and undercuts the strong framing of a strict >50% guarantee.

strengths: The paper gives a clear and timely formulation of LLM alignment with general preferences as a two-player zero-sum game and highlights the limitation of KL-regularized Nash equilibria for robust alignment.

It proposes a simple meta-algorithm, COMAL, based on the conceptual prox method and shows that many existing preference optimization methods can be interpreted as computing the prox operator, enabling black-box integration.

The theoretical analysis provides last-iterate convergence guarantees to an exact Nash equilibrium under exact regularized-game solutions and extends to approximate solutions with explicit error conditions.
The synthetic experiments clearly illustrate known cycling/divergence of MD, iterative DPO, IPO, and SPPO in an intransitive preference game, while COMAL converges in the last iterate.
The LLM-based experiments suggest COMAL can improve stability and achieve win rates above 50% against several iterative baselines on their setup.
weaknesses: The LLM evaluation is circular: the same preference oracle used to generate training preference labels is also used as the evaluator, which can inflate win rates and does not establish alignment with true human or independent preferences.

The LLM experiments likely use a Bradley-Terry-style reward model as the oracle, so they do not actually test the paper's central motivation of general, non-transitive preferences in the large-scale setting.

The practical COMAL implementation deviates substantially from Algorithm 4: the reference policy is updated heuristically when training 'begins to converge or overfit', and inner solvers are not run to the accuracy required by the theory, leaving the theoretical guarantees disconnected from the experiments.

Missing strong and obvious baselines: SPPO, Nash-MD, DNO, REBEL, DRO, Mirror-Prox, and OMWU are discussed or implementable but not compared in the LLM experiments, even though OMWU also has last-iterate convergence guarantees in zero-sum games.
The empirical gains are small and not supported by statistical significance tests or error bars; for example COMAL beats INPO-Small by only 51.30% in Table 2, which could easily be noise.

The claim of being the first to achieve last-iterate convergence to an exact Nash equilibrium in LLM alignment is overclaimed, since the paper itself shows OMWU/Mirror-Prox can be implemented for the same unregularized game with existing preference methods, though it leaves them untested.

Reproducibility is limited: no code is provided, the number of inner iterations K_t and stopping criteria are unclear, hyperparameter selection is not fully specified, and only one model size, dataset, and preference oracle are used.

Robust alignment is only tested against seven checkpoints; there is no evaluation against adversarial policies, external strong models such as GPT-4, or human raters, so the claimed 50% win-rate guarantee is not empirically validated.
The synthetic experiment is a simple 3x3 bandit and mostly confirms known cycling behavior in mirror descent; it is not sufficient to validate the method's practical value for LLM alignment.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: robust alignment with general, possibly intransitive human preferences, where the Nash equilibrium policy guarantees at least a 50% win rate against any competitor.

Provides a clear theoretical contribution: COMAL is proved to achieve last-iterate convergence to an exact Nash equilibrium of the unregularized zero-sum game, unlike prior iterative preference optimization methods that diverge or converge only to a KL-regularized Nash equilibrium.

The meta-algorithm is elegant and modular: many existing methods (PPO, DPO, IPO, SPPO, INPO, etc.) can be interpreted as computing the prox operator and thus integrated into COMAL with minimal changes.
Synthetic experiments are well-designed for the claim: they clearly illustrate divergence/cycling of MD, iterative DPO, iterative IPO, and SPPO, while COMAL converges to the unique Nash equilibrium.

LLM experiments on Qwen2-1.5B and UltraFeedback are substantial in iteration count (up to 42 iterations) and show COMAL maintaining win rates above 50% against all compared checkpoints, with better last-checkpoint stability.
The paper is generally well-written and clearly positions itself relative to RLHF, DPO, IPO, Nash-MD, SPPO, INPO, and related game-theoretic literature.
weaknesses: The main theorem relies on a non-trivial support assumption: there exists an exact Nash equilibrium with the same support as the SFT policy. This may not hold in realistic LLM alignment settings and is not empirically verified.

The approximate-solver convergence guarantee requires inner-solver error decreasing as O(1/t^4), which is extremely stringent and not practically enforceable in large-scale LLM training. The theory-practice gap is significant.

The practical implementation deviates from the idealized meta-algorithm: it uses finite inner optimization steps and a heuristic reference-update schedule ('when the first optimization step begins to converge or overfit'), with no ablation on update frequency, inner steps, τ, or approximation error.

LLM evaluation is limited to a single 1.5B model, one dataset, and no independent/human evaluation. The same preference oracle is used both for generating training preference data and for evaluation, which risks inflated or circular win-rate measurements.

The reported LLM win-rate advantages are modest (e.g., 51.30% against INPO-Small), and no confidence intervals or statistical significance tests are provided, making it hard to judge how reliable the empirical gains are.
Important general-preference baselines such as Nash-MD, SPPO, and DNO are not compared in the LLM experiments, even though they are directly relevant to the claimed robust-alignment setting.

The 'first' last-iterate convergence claim is plausible within LLM alignment, but the paper does not fully discuss whether similar guarantees already exist in the game-theoretic optimization literature under comparable assumptions.

strengths: Addresses an important and well-motivated problem: the inability of the Bradley–Terry assumption, and hence of RLHF/DPO-style pipelines, to represent intransitive/general preferences, and the failure of existing MD-based self-play methods (iterative DPO/IPO, SPPO, INPO) to attain the exact Nash equilibrium of the alignment game.

The theoretical contribution is non-trivial and clearly beyond the state of the art: last-iterate convergence to the unregularized Nash equilibrium (Theorem 1), an extension to inexactly solved regularized games with accuracy t^{-4} (Theorem 3), and a linear-rate MWU result for the inner regularized game (Theorem 2, with a self-contained proof). Relaxing the 'bounded log density' condition to a support-matching assumption on the Nash equilibrium (Assumption 1) is a genuine improvement, and the proofs (Lemma 2, Corollary 2, Lemma 3, Lemma 4, Pinsker/three-point identities) are carefully executed.

The synthetic 3x3 intransitive game (Fig. 1a, 3, 4) is a crisp and convincing diagnostic: it clearly shows divergence/cycling of MD-style methods and the constant equilibrium gap of INPO (a KL-regularized solution), while CO... converges to the true Nash. This directly corroborates the theory and is the most convincing evidence in the paper.

The observation that a wide range of existing losses (PPO, GRPO, DPO, IPO, SPPO, INPO, DRO, REBEL) can be interpreted as instantiations of the prox operator, and the resulting plug-and-play recipes (Algorithms 3–11), provides a useful unifying view and makes the method easy to adopt with minimal changes to existing pipelines.

The empirical study is substantial in effort (Llama-3-8B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B, plus a 1.5B study in Appendix K; 18 iterations, ~100 A6000-GPU-hours per algorithm) and includes both a controlled oracle evaluation and a standard-benchmark sanity check (Table 3), reporting that no general capability is lost.

Comparisons are made against a sensible set of baselines, including the closest prior work INPO as well as Iter-IPO with tuned KL strengths; the paper is generous to baselines by reporting their best checkpoints (Table 1) and also reports final-checkpoint comparisons (Table 6) where CO... fares even better.

Positioning and related work are thorough and honest, including explicit discussion of concurrent/subsequent work (Wang et al. 2025, Zhou et al. 2025, Tiapkin et al. 2025) and a candid Limitations section about non-convexity, the lack of a provable guarantee in LLM practice, and the absence of a convergence rate.
weaknesses: The LLM-level evidence for the central 'general preference' claim is indirect. The preference oracle is a 50/50 mixture of two BT reward models (Skywork-Reward-Llama-3.1-8B and ArmoRM-Llama3-8B), which is a mild form of non-BT preference; no verification is given that the resulting pairwise preferences on the UltraFeedback data are actually intransitive, nor how large the intransitivity is. A demonstration with a genuinely intransitive or human-annotated preference signal (or a synthetic-but-realistic intransitivity injected into LLM training) would be far more persuasive.

Evaluation is self-referential: the model is trained to fit the oracle and evaluated against the same oracle on AlpacaEval prompts. The headline '>60.2% / >56.8% win rate against all compared algorithms' therefore measures agreement with the training oracle rather than genuine preference alignment. The only external checks (Table 3, GPT-4 judged AlpacaEval/Arena-Hard) show CO... essentially on par with baselines (e.g., Arena-Hard 41.3 vs Iter-IPO 43.8; AlpacaEval 53.5 vs INPO 51.6), and the paper concedes it loses to Iter-IPO on Arena-Hard. In other words, the practical payoff of unregularized-Nash convergence is not clearly demonstrated under an independent evaluator.

Theory–practice disconnect: Theorem 3 requires each regularized game to be solved to accuracy eps_t = O(c1^2/(9t^4)), which is far stronger than what is realized by the practical instantiation (only T=3 outer rounds, with the reference policy updated every 6 INPO iterations in the Llama runs). The asymptotic guarantees therefore do not explain the observed gains, and the paper offers no finite-iteration bound or diagnostic (e.g., measured duality gap or distance-to-Nash under the oracle) to bridge the gap.

Statistical rigor is limited: results are reported as point-estimate win rates with no confidence intervals, seeds/variance, or significance tests, yet margins over the strongest iterative baselines are moderate (60.25% and 62.98% against Iter-IPO in Table 1; 56.89%/57.89% against Iter-IPO/INPO in Table 2). It is hard to judge whether these margins are robust.

Fairness/comparability of hyperparameters: the tuning protocol differs across methods (e.g., eta^{-1} changed from 0.002 to 0.1 mid-training for CO... and for the 'long' baselines; baselines reported at their best checkpoint while CO... is reported at its final checkpoint in Table 1). While the paper argues this is generous to baselines, the resulting numbers mix 'best' and 'final' checkpoints and make the average column hard to interpret.

Novelty of the algorithm itself is moderate: the meta-algorithm is essentially the conceptual Prox-method / iterative-regularization proximal-point scheme with the reference policy updated to the latest iterate, which is close to existing iterative-DPO-style recipes and to concurrent work (Wang et al. 2025; Zhou et al. 2025) that also demonstrate last-iterate convergence in this setting. The authors' claim of being 'first' is hedged in a footnote and depends on the 'approximate solver' refinement, so the algorithmic advance is incremental relative to the well-established prox-method literature; the main contribution is the theoretical relaxation plus the practical recipes.

Minor presentation/consistency issues: e.g., Algorithm 9 states 'defined in Algorithm 6' where it should refer to Algorithm 8, and the appendix is dense enough that key practical guidance (how many outer rounds, how the reference-policy update triggers are chosen) is somewhat buried; no code/artifact link is mentioned, which weakens reproducibility despite the detailed hyperparameter reporting.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: alignment under general, potentially intransitive human preferences, where Bradley-Terry assumptions are insufficient.

Provides a theoretical framework for last-iterate convergence to an unregularized Nash equilibrium, including analysis for approximately solved regularized games, which is a nontrivial extension of conceptual prox ideas to LLM alignment.

The COMAL meta-algorithm is simple and flexible: it can be integrated with many existing preference-optimization methods (PPO, DPO, IPO, INPO, etc.) by viewing them as prox-operator implementations, requiring minimal changes to existing pipelines.

Synthetic experiments clearly illustrate the cycling/divergence behavior of mirror-descent-style methods such as iterative DPO, iterative IPO, and SPPO on an intransitive 3x3 game, while COMAL converges to the Nash equilibrium.

LLM experiments cover two model families (Llama-3-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B), a large instruction dataset, multiple baselines, controlled oracle-based evaluation, and standard benchmark sanity checks.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: COMAL is essentially the conceptual prox/proximal point method from game theory applied to LLM alignment. The theoretical results adapt known last-iterate convergence guarantees for monotone games, and the claim of being the first algorithm with last-iterate convergence to the unregularized Nash equilibrium is overstated because Mirror-Prox and OMWU already have such guarantees and are only deferred to future work.

The empirical evaluation is incomplete for a top-tier AI conference. Key general-preference and self-play baselines such as Nash-MD, SPPO, DNO, REBEL, DRO, Online IPO, and the paper's own Mirror-Prox/OMWU implementations are not compared in the main LLM experiments. Only INPO and iterative IPO are used as primary iterative baselines.

The main win-rate results are obtained using the same preference oracle for both training and evaluation. This makes the primary comparisons circular/controlled: COMAL is explicitly optimizing the oracle's win rate, so improvements on this metric are expected and do not by themselves demonstrate better alignment with real human preferences.

On standard benchmarks with external evaluators (e.g., GPT-4 for AlpacaEval and Arena-Hard), COMAL is not consistently better than iterative IPO or INPO and is sometimes slightly worse (e.g., Arena-Hard for Llama-3 and Qwen2.5). This weakens the claim of broad practical effectiveness and generalizability.

There is a substantial gap between theory and practice. The convergence guarantee requires solving each regularized game exactly or to a sufficiently small approximation error, but the practical LLM implementation uses INPO with limited inner iterations and nonconvex loss minimization. The observed gains may therefore stem from the KL-regularization schedule and periodic reference-policy updates rather than the guaranteed outer-loop convergence.

The theoretical assumptions are restrictive for LLM alignment: the analysis assumes the existence of a Nash equilibrium with exactly the same support as the initial policy and restricts the policy class to that support. It also provides only asymptotic outer-loop convergence, with no practical finite-time rate or clear guidance on how many inner iterations are needed in realistic settings.

Baseline tuning and checkpoint selection may favor COMAL: COMAL is evaluated at its final checkpoint while iterative IPO and INPO are often evaluated at their best checkpoints due to later degradation, and different regularization schedules are used. There is no statistical significance analysis, confidence intervals, or systematic control for hyperparameter search across methods.

Reproducibility is only partially supported. The paper does not provide code or a detailed enough description of the exact training setup, random seeds, data splits, or compute budgets to fully reproduce the LLM experiments, and several appendix algorithm tables are incomplete or garbled.

strengths: Addresses an important limitation of Bradley-Terry-based RLHF by modeling alignment as a general-preference two-player zero-sum game and targeting Nash equilibrium policies with 50% win-rate guarantees.

Provides a simple meta-algorithm COMAL that can be integrated with existing preference optimization methods, with theoretical last-iterate convergence to the unregularized Nash equilibrium, including an approximate-solver analysis.
Synthetic experiments clearly illustrate the divergent or biased behavior of MD-style baselines and INPO, while COMAL converges to the true Nash equilibrium.
LLM experiments on Llama-3-8B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B show consistent win rates above 60.2% and 56.8% against compared baselines, and standard benchmarks suggest no severe alignment tax.
Offers a useful unified view of several preference optimization methods as implementations of the prox operator and provides concrete instantiations with INPO, GRPO, SPPO, DRO, and REBEL.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental: COMAL is primarily an application of the conceptual prox/proximal-point method from game theory to LLM alignment, with the practical changes largely involving periodic reference-policy updates.
The LLM evaluation omits important baselines such as SPPO and Nash-MD, which are directly related to general-preference alignment and last-iterate convergence, weakening the empirical comparison.

The preference oracle is a mixture of two Bradley-Terry reward models; although controlled, this may not fully capture complex intransitive human preferences, and using the same oracle for training and evaluation limits external validity.

Theoretical guarantees rely on Assumption 1 (existence of a Nash equilibrium with the same support as the initial policy) and on solving each regularized game to high accuracy, assumptions that are not guaranteed in practical LLM training.

Some experimental reporting is unclear: tables omit rows for some compared algorithms, and COMAL is sometimes evaluated at its final checkpoint while baselines are reported at their best checkpoints, complicating interpretation.
